items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon Problem Encounter the Phenomenon, Make Your Claim: A nuclear power plant on the coast produces electricity from a few kilograms of fuel per day. Use your CER chart to make a claim about where the plant's energy comes from and how it is released.

body.html: No data are given; we need a testable one-sentence claim that will be refined at the end of the module.

In a fission reactor a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 splits into two middle-sized nuclei that are more tightly bound per nucleon. The products have less total mass than the starting nuclei, and the lost mass appears as energy through 𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>.

Evidence to collect: (1) binding energy per nucleon is less negative for very heavy nuclei than for nuclei near 𝐴= 100 to 140 (Lesson 1); (2) a nuclear reaction releases the energy equivalent of the mass that disappears (Lesson 2); (3) neutrons released by one fission can cause more fissions, so a controlled chain reaction keeps the plant running (Lesson 2).

answer.html: The plant's energy comes from fission of uranium-235: a neutron splits the nucleus into two smaller, more tightly bound nuclei plus extra neutrons, and the small loss of mass is released as about 180 MeV of energy per fission. Absorbing rods keep the chain reaction steady.

check.html: The claim can be tested: the energy per fission follows from the mass difference of reactants and products.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon, Ask Questions: Write three new questions about the nuclear power plant that could go on the driving question board.

body.html: Good driving questions can be answered by measurements, calculations, or models.
Think about what must be true for the plant to work: how the reaction is started, how it is kept from running away, and how much energy it really gives per kilogram of fuel.

answer.html: (1) Why does a slow neutron cause fission better than a fast one? (2) How can the reaction rate be controlled, and how can it be shut down quickly? (3) How much energy does one kilogram of uranium-235 release compared with one kilogram of coal?

check.html: Each question is answered by a later part of the module (moderators and control rods, fission energy, mass- energy conversion).

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 3: Identify the mass number and the electric charge of each nucleus: lithium with 3 protons and 3 neutrons; lithium with 3 protons and 4 neutrons; beryllium with 4 protons and 3 neutrons; beryllium with 4 protons and 5 neutrons; boron with 5 protons and 5 neutrons.

body.html: The proton and neutron count for each nucleus is given above. Find 𝐴 and the charge.
Mass number 𝐴 = protons + neutrons. Charge = 𝑍𝑒, where 𝑍 is the number of protons.
Add the nucleons in each nucleus, then multiply the proton count by +𝑒. Nucleus Protons Neutrons
Charge Lithium-6 3 3 6
Lithium-7 3 4 7
Beryllium-7 4 3 7
Beryllium-9 4 5 9
Boron-10 5 5 10

answer.html: Li: 𝐴= 6 and 7, charge +3𝑒; Be: 𝐴= 7 and 9, charge +4𝑒; B: 𝐴= 10, charge +5𝑒.

check.html: The two lithium nuclei are isotopes with the same charge; Li-7 and Be-7 have the same 𝐴 but different charge, so they are different elements.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 674): Compare and contrast potassium-39 and potassium-40.

body.html: Potassium has 𝑍= 19. Potassium-39 has 𝐴= 39; potassium-40 has 𝐴= 40.
Isotopes have the same 𝑍 but different numbers of neutrons, 𝑁= 𝐴−𝑍.

Neutrons: 39 −19 = 20 for K-39 and 40 −19 = 21 for K-40. Both have 19 protons and (when neutral) 19 electrons, so the chemistry is the same. K-40 is radioactive (half-life about 1.3 × 10<sup>9</sup> years) while K-39 is stable.

answer.html: Alike: 19 protons, 19 electrons, same chemical behavior. Different: K-39 has 20 neutrons and is stable; K-40 has 21 neutrons, a slightly larger mass, and is radioactive.

check.html: Same element means the same 𝑍; only 𝑁 and 𝐴 differ.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 674): Explain what a weighted average is and how it determines an element's atomic mass. Illustrate with natural boron, which is 19.9% boron-10 and 80.1% boron-11 (use mass numbers 10 and 11 as the masses).

body.html: Abundances 0.199 and 0.801; masses 10 and 11.
A weighted average multiplies each value by its fractional share of the total and adds the results.

answer.html: A weighted average counts each value in proportion to how often it occurs. An element's atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of its natural isotopes, so it need not be a whole number. For boron this gives about 10.8 u (the listed value is 10.81 u).

check.html: 10.8 lies between 10 and 11, nearer 11, because boron-11 is more abundant.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 1: Three isotopes of lead have mass numbers 206, 207, and 208. Lead has 𝑍= 82. How many neutrons are in each nucleus?

body.html: 𝐴= 𝑍+ 𝑁, so 𝑁= 𝐴−𝑍.

answer.html: Pb-206 has 124 neutrons, Pb-207 has 125, and Pb-208 has 126.

check.html: Each extra nucleon in the same element is an extra neutron.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 2: How many neutrons are in an atom of gold-197,

body.html: 𝐴= 197, 𝑍= 79. Find 𝑁.
𝑁= 𝐴−𝑍.

answer.html: 118 neutrons.

check.html: Heavy nuclei have more neutrons than protons (118 > 79).

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 3: How many neutrons are in phosphorus-32? (Use the periodic table for 𝑍.)

body.html: 𝐴= 32; phosphorus has 𝑍= 15 (periodic table).
𝑁= 𝐴−𝑍.

answer.html: 17 neutrons.

check.html: Stable phosphorus-31 has 16 neutrons, so one more for phosphorus-32 is reasonable.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 4 (Challenge): Lithium has 𝑍= 3. Write the symbol 𝑍

body.html: 𝑍= 3; 𝑁= 3, 4, 5. Find 𝐴 for each and write the symbols.
𝐴= 𝑍+ 𝑁. The notation is <sub>𝑍</sub> <sup>𝐴</sup>X, with the mass number on top and the proton number below.

answer.html: <sub>3</sub> <sup>6</sup>Li (3 neutrons), <sub>3</sub> <sup>7</sup>Li (4 neutrons), <sub>3</sub> <sup>8</sup>Li (5 neutrons).

check.html: The subscript is always 3 for lithium.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 675): Explain what a mass defect is. Illustrate with beryllium-9 (4 protons, 5 neutrons), whose atomic mass is 9.012183 u.

body.html: 𝑍= 4, 𝑁= 5; 𝑚= 9.012183 u. Find the mass defect.
A bound nucleus has less mass than its separated nucleons because the binding energy has left the system (𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>). Use hydrogen atoms for the protons so the electrons are counted.

answer.html: The mass defect is the amount by which a nucleus's (atom's) mass is less than the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons. For beryllium-9 it is −0.062442 u.

check.html: The sign is negative in the module's convention (assembled minus parts).

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 676): Explain what binding energy is. Find the binding energy of lithium-7 (3 protons, 4 neutrons), whose atomic mass is 7.016003 u.

body.html: Work must be done against the strong force to pull a nucleus apart, so the separated nucleons have more energy than the assembled nucleus. That difference is the binding energy, equal to the mass defect times 931.49 MeV/u.

answer.html: Binding energy is the energy difference between the separated nucleons and the assembled nucleus (the energy needed to pull the nucleus completely apart), written as a negative number. For lithium-7 it is −39.25 MeV.

check.html: −39.25 / 7 = −5.61 MeV per nucleon, a sensible value for a light nucleus on the binding-energy curve.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 676): Explain the meaning and importance of 𝐸= 931.49 MeV/u. Use it to find the energy equivalent of a mass of 0.0250 u in both MeV and joules (1 u = 1.6605 × 10−27 kg).

body.html: 𝑚= 0.0250 u. Find 𝐸 in MeV and J.
From 𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>, a mass of 1 u is equivalent to 931.49 MeV, or 1.4924 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> J.

answer.html: 931.49 MeV/u is a conversion factor between mass in u and energy in MeV. It is important because mass defects are measured in u, and multiplying by this factor gives binding energy directly without converting to kilograms and joules. A mass of 0.0250 u is equivalent to 23.3 MeV (3.73 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>12</sup> J).

check.html: Units: u × MeV/u = MeV, and 23.3 MeV × 1.60 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>13</sup> J/MeV = 3.73 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>12</sup> J.

items.title: Calculate its mass defect. (b) Calculate its binding energy.

body.html: Use hydrogen atoms (proton plus electron) so the electrons are counted correctly. Defect = atom mass − parts; 𝐸= (defect)(931.49 MeV/u).

answer.html: (a) −0.172460 u; (b) −160.6 MeV (about −8.03 MeV per nucleon).

check.html: The per-nucleon value is near the −8 MeV on the binding-energy curve for 𝐴= 20.

items.title: Calculate its mass defect. (b) Calculate its binding energy.

body.html: Same method as above.

answer.html: (a) −0.034347 u; (b) −31.99 MeV (about −5.33 MeV per nucleon).

check.html: Light nuclei have smaller binding energy per nucleon than mid-sized ones, as on the binding-energy curve.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Mass Defect) 7: Fluorine-19, 9

question.html: <sup>19</sup>F, has a mass defect of −0.158672 u. (a) Calculate the mass of the fluorine-19 atom. (b) Calculate its binding energy.

body.html: Rearrange 𝛥𝑚= 𝑚−𝑚<sub>parts</sub> to get 𝑚= 𝑚<sub>parts</sub> + 𝛥𝑚.

check.html: The mass is close to the mass number 19, and −147.8 / 19 = −7.78 MeV per nucleon is reasonable.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Mass Defect) 8 (Challenge): Magnesium-24, 12

question.html: <sup>24</sup>Mg, has a mass of 23.985042 u and magnesium-26, <sub>12</sub> <sup>26</sup>Mg, has a mass of 25.982593 u. (a) Find the mass defect of each. (b) Find the binding energy of each. (c) Why are the binding energies different?

body.html: Same method; the larger nucleus contains more nucleons.

answer.html: (a) Mg-24: −0.212838 u; Mg-26: −0.232617 u. (b) Mg-24: −198.3 MeV; Mg-26: −216.7 MeV. (c) The binding energies differ because the nuclei contain different numbers of nucleons: Mg-26 has two more neutrons, so more strong-force attractions and a larger total binding energy. Per nucleon the values are close (−8.26 versus −8.33 MeV); the extra neutrons add attraction without adding proton repulsion.

check.html: Both per-nucleon values are near the −8 MeV shown on the binding-energy curve for 𝐴 in the 20s.

items.title: Nucleus 𝐴 Average binding energy per nucleon

body.html: Compare the values for 𝐴= 120 and 𝐴= 222.
Binding energy per nucleon is most negative near 𝐴= 56 and becomes less negative for heavier nuclei.
𝐴= 120 is closer to the minimum of the curve than 𝐴= 222 is, so | −8.51 | > | −7.69|.

answer.html: Tin-120 has the larger magnitude (8.51 MeV per nucleon versus 7.69 MeV for radon-222).

check.html: Radon-222 is large and radioactive, consistent with being less tightly bound per nucleon.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 9: Aluminum-27, 13

question.html: <sup>27</sup>Al, has a mass of 26.981539 u. Find its mass defect and binding energy.

body.html: Same hydrogen-atom method.

answer.html: Mass defect −0.241496 u; binding energy −224.9 MeV.

check.html: −224.9 / 27 = −8.33 MeV per nucleon, in line with the binding-energy curve.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 10: How are the nuclei in each pair alike and different? Pair 1: nitrogen-14 and nitrogen-15. Pair 2: nitrogen-15 and oxygen-15. (Nitrogen 𝑍= 7, oxygen 𝑍= 8.)

body.html: Count protons and neutrons: N-14 (7 p, 7 n); N-15 (7 p, 8 n); O-15 (8 p, 7 n).
Same 𝑍 means the same element (isotopes). Same 𝐴 with different 𝑍 means different elements.
Pair 1 has equal proton numbers and different neutron numbers. Pair 2 has equal mass numbers (𝐴= 15) and different proton numbers.

answer.html: Pair 1 are isotopes of the same element (both nitrogen, 𝑍= 7) with different masses (7 versus 8 neutrons). Pair 2 share the mass number 15 but are different elements (nitrogen and oxygen), with the numbers of protons and neutrons swapped (7 p, 8 n versus 8 p, 7 n).

check.html: Pair 1 nuclei differ by one nucleon; pair 2 nuclei have the same number of nucleons.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 11: Nitrogen-13 (7 protons, 6 neutrons, mass 13.005739 u) decays by positron emission into carbon-13 (6 protons, 7 neutrons, mass 13.003355 u). Which nucleus has the more negative binding energy? Explain.

body.html: Use 𝑚<sub>H</sub> = 1.007825 u and 𝑚<sub>n</sub> = 1.008665 u.
Compare the binding energies from the hydrogen-atom method.

answer.html: Carbon-13 has the more negative binding energy (−97.11 MeV versus −94.10 MeV). Nitrogen-13 has one more proton, so more electric repulsion inside the nucleus, which lowers its binding energy and makes it less stable.

check.html: The decay turns the less tightly bound nucleus into the more tightly bound one.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 12: Nitrogen-13 has a mass defect of −0.101026 u and carbon-13 has a mass defect of −0.104250 u. Which has the larger mass defect?

body.html: Mass defect is the mass equivalent of the binding energy, so the more tightly bound nucleus has the larger defect in magnitude.
| −0.104250 | > | −0.101026|, so carbon-13's defect is larger.

answer.html: Carbon-13, with a mass defect of −0.104250 u versus −0.101026 u for nitrogen-13.

check.html: Consistent with carbon-13 having the larger-magnitude binding energy.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 13: A student says a nucleus with 100 protons should be more stable than one with 50 protons because it has more nucleons pulling on each other. Explain why the student's reasoning fails.

body.html: The strong force has a very short range, so each nucleon is attracted only by its few nearest neighbors. The electric repulsion has long range, so each proton is repelled by every other proton in the nucleus.

Adding nucleons beyond a certain size does not give each nucleon more strong-force neighbors, but each added proton adds a repulsion with every other proton. The number of proton-proton repulsions grows roughly as 𝑍<sup>2</sup>: about 50<sup>2</sup> = 2500 for 50 protons and 100<sup>2</sup> = 10, 000 for 100, four times as many.

answer.html: The attraction per nucleon stays about the same (only nearest neighbors count), while the total repulsion grows much faster with the number of protons. In very large nuclei the repulsion wins, so the 100-proton nucleus is less stable, not more.

check.html: All known nuclei with a large number of protons are radioactive.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 14: Use the binding energy per nucleon values Mg-24: −8.26 MeV, Cr-48: −8.57 MeV, Fe-56: −8.79 MeV, and a nucleus of 𝐴= 112: −8.50 MeV. (a) Would fusing two Mg-24 nuclei into Cr-48 release or absorb energy, and how much? (b) Would fusing two Fe-56 nuclei into an 𝐴= 112 nucleus release or absorb energy, and how much? (c) What does this tell you about where energy-releasing fusion in stars stops?

body.html: Total binding energy = (number of nucleons)(binding energy per nucleon). Compare before and after.
Fusion releases energy only if the product has a more negative total binding energy than the reactants.
The change is −411.4 −( −396.5) = −14.9 MeV (more bound, so energy is released). 𝐸<sub>before</sub> = 2(56)( −8.79) = −984.5 MeV,
The change is −952.0 −( −984.5) = + 32.5 MeV (less bound, so energy must be supplied).

answer.html: (a) Energy is released, about 15 MeV. (b) Energy is absorbed, about 32 MeV. (c) Beyond iron-56 ( 𝑍= 26) the curve rises, so fusion stops releasing energy; stars cannot get energy by fusing nuclei heavier than iron.

check.html: Fe-56 sits at the bottom of the curve, so neither fusing nor splitting it releases energy.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: Make Your Claim

question.html: Use your CER chart to make a claim about how the Sun produces energy and how we can replicate it.

body.html: No data are given; we need a testable one-sentence claim to be refined at the end of the module.
The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion: light nuclei combine into a more tightly bound nucleus, and the lost mass appears as energy through 𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>.

The module's evidence is: (1) binding energy per nucleon is more negative near iron than for hydrogen (Lesson 1), (2) mass lost in a nuclear reaction is released as energy (Lesson 2), and (3) fusion needs very high temperature to overcome the repulsion between nuclei (Lesson 2).

answer.html: The Sun fuses four hydrogen nuclei into one helium-4 nucleus (the proton-proton chain), releasing about 25 MeV per helium nucleus because the product has less mass than the four protons. We could replicate it by heating hydrogen isotopes to well over 10 million kelvin and confining the hot plasma (for example with magnetic fields) long enough for fusion to occur.

check.html: The claim is testable: the mass difference and the 25 MeV figure can be computed from nuclear masses.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: Ask Questions

question.html: Do you have other questions about the phenomenon? Add them to the driving question board.

body.html: Good driving questions can be answered by measurements, calculations, or models.

Questions tied to the picture of the Sun: Why do nuclei need such high temperature to fuse? Why does fusion release energy but fission of uranium does too? How much mass does the Sun lose each second?

answer.html: (1) Why must the fusing nuclei have so much thermal energy? (2) Why does fusing small nuclei and splitting large nuclei both release energy? (3) How can a fusion plasma be contained without touching the walls?

check.html: Each question is answered by a later part of the module (binding energy curve, Coulomb repulsion, magnetic confinement).

items.title: Lesson 1, Launch Lab "A Nuclear Model" and "Identify Crosscutting Concepts"

question.html: Use a model to investigate forces between protons and neutrons; make a table of crosscutting concepts with examples.

body.html: These are online/hands-on activities; no data are provided here.
The nuclear model balances the attractive strong force (acting only between neighbors) against the repulsive electric force between protons (acting across the whole nucleus).

Expected result of the model: nuclei with a good balance of neutrons and protons stay together; too many protons make the electric repulsion win. Sample crosscutting-concept table entries: Crosscutting concept Example from Lesson 1 Scale, proportion, quantity Nucleus is about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>14</sup> m across; atom is about 10,000 times larger Energy and matter Mass defect is the mass equivalent of binding energy Patterns Binding energy per nucleon is most negative near 𝐴= 56 Structure and function Neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electric repulsion Stability and change Isotopes with too many or too few neutrons are unstable

answer.html: Representative results are given above (labeled as expected, since the activity itself is done online).

check.html: Each example is something stated in the lesson text.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 3: Identify the mass number and electric charge of each nucleus

body.html: Figure 3 shows (reading the labels): hydrogen with 1 p and 0 n; 1 p and 1 n; 1 p and 2 n; helium with 2 p and 1 n; 2 p and 2 n. Find 𝐴 and charge.
Mass number 𝐴 = protons + neutrons. Charge = 𝑍𝑒, where 𝑍 is the number of protons.
Add the nucleons in each picture; multiply the protons by +𝑒. Nucleus Protons Neutrons
Charge Hydrogen-1 1 0 1
Hydrogen-2 1 1 2
Hydrogen-3 1 2 3
Helium-3 2 1 3
Helium-4 2 2 4

answer.html: H: 𝐴= 1, 2, 3 with charge +𝑒 each; He: 𝐴= 3, 4 with charge +2𝑒 each.

check.html: Isotopes of one element share the same charge.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 674): Compare and contrast carbon-12 and carbon-14

body.html: Carbon: 𝑍= 6. Carbon-12 has 𝐴= 12; carbon-14 has 𝐴= 14.
Isotopes have the same 𝑍 but different numbers of neutrons.

Neutrons: 12 −6 = 6 for C-12; 14 −6 = 8 for C-14. Both have 6 protons and 6 electrons when neutral, so the chemistry is the same. C-14 is heavier and is radioactive (half-life 5730 years); C-12 is stable.

answer.html: Alike: 6 protons, 6 electrons, same chemical behavior. Different: C-12 has 6 neutrons and is stable; C-14 has 8 neutrons, a larger mass, and is radioactive.

check.html: Same element, so same 𝑍; only 𝑁 and 𝐴 differ.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 674): Explain what a weighted average is and how it determines an element's atomic mass

body.html: A weighted average counts each value in proportion to how often it occurs.

Multiply each isotope's mass by its fractional abundance and add. Example (abundances from outside the book): chlorine is about 75.8% Cl-35 and 24.2% Cl-37, so 0.758(35) + 0.242(37) ≈35.5 u, close to the listed 35.453 u.

answer.html: A weighted average multiplies each value by its share of the total before adding. An element's atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of its naturally occurring isotopes' masses, so it need not be a whole number.

check.html: The result (35.5 u) lies between 35 and 37, nearer 35, because Cl-35 is more abundant.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 1: Neutrons in uranium isotopes

question.html: Three uranium isotopes have mass numbers 234, 235, 238; 𝑍= 92. How many neutrons in each?

body.html: 𝐴= 𝑍+ 𝑁, so 𝑁= 𝐴−𝑍.

answer.html: U-234 has 142 neutrons, U-235 has 143, U-238 has 146.

check.html: More nucleons with the same protons means more neutrons.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 2: Neutrons in mercury-200

body.html: 𝐴= 200, 𝑍= 80. Find 𝑁.
𝑁= 𝐴−𝑍.

answer.html: 120 neutrons.

check.html: Heavy nuclei have more neutrons than protons (120 > 80).

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 3: Neutrons in oxygen-15

body.html: 𝐴= 15; oxygen has 𝑍= 8 (periodic table).
𝑁= 𝐴−𝑍.

answer.html: 7 neutrons.

check.html: Oxygen-16 has 8 neutrons, so one fewer for oxygen-15 is reasonable.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Isotopes) 4 (Challenge): Symbols of the three hydrogen isotopes

body.html: Hydrogen 𝑍= 1; neutrons = 0, 1, 2.
𝐴= 𝑍+ 𝑁, so 𝐴= 1, 2, 3. The notation is <sub>𝑍</sub>

check.html: Subscript is always 1 for hydrogen.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 675): Explain what a mass defect is

body.html: A bound nucleus has less mass than its separated nucleons because the binding energy has left the system (via 𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>).
Mass defect = (mass of the assembled nucleus) − (sum of masses of its separate nucleons). For helium- 4 this is 4.002603 −4.031882 = −0.029279 u.

answer.html: The mass defect is the amount by which a nucleus's mass is less than the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons.

check.html: It is negative in the book's sign convention (assembled minus parts).

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 676): Explain what binding energy is

body.html: Pulling a nucleon out of a nucleus requires work against the strong force.
Separated nucleons have more energy than the assembled nucleus. The difference is the binding energy.

answer.html: Binding energy is the energy difference between the separated nucleons and the assembled nucleus (the energy needed to pull the nucleus completely apart); it is the energy equivalent of the mass defect, and is written as a negative number.

check.html: A larger magnitude means a more tightly bound nucleus.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 676): Meaning and importance of 𝐸= 931.49 MeV/u

body.html: From 𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>, a mass of 1 u = 1.6605 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>27</sup> kg has energy 1.4924 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> J = 931.49 MeV.
The equation says each atomic mass unit of mass is equivalent to 931.49 MeV of energy.

answer.html: It is a conversion factor between mass in u and energy in MeV. It is important because mass defects are measured in u, and multiplying by 931.49 MeV/u gives binding energies directly without converting to kilograms and joules.

check.html: Units: u × MeV/u = MeV.

check.html: Per-nucleon value agrees with Figure 6 for 𝐴= 12 (about −7.7 MeV).

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problems (Mass Defect) 8 (Challenge): Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18

question.html: <sub>8</sub> <sup>16</sup>O has mass 15.994915 u; <sub>8</sub> <sup>18</sup>O has mass 17.999160 u.

body.html: O-16: 8 p, 8 n. O-18: 8 p, 10 n. Find the defect and binding energy of each, and explain the difference.
Same method; the larger nucleus contains more nucleons.

answer.html: (a) O-16: −0.137005 u; O-18: −0.150090 u. (b) O-16: −127.6 MeV; O-18: −139.8 MeV. (c) The binding energies differ because the nuclei contain different numbers of nucleons: O-18 has two more neutrons, so more strong-force attractions and a larger total binding energy. Per nucleon, though, O-18 is slightly less tightly bound (−7.77 versus −7.98 MeV), because the two extra neutrons upset the equal balance of protons and neutrons.

check.html: Both per-nucleon values are near the −8 MeV found in Figure 6.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 6 "Infer": Which has the larger-magnitude average binding energy per nucleon, 52

body.html: Figure 6 (read): the curve is about −8.7 MeV near 𝐴= 130 and about −7.6 MeV at 𝐴= 236.
Binding energy per nucleon is most negative near 𝐴= 56 and becomes less negative for heavier nuclei.
𝐴= 131 is closer to the minimum of the curve than 𝐴= 236 is.

answer.html: Iodine-131 has the larger magnitude (about 8.7 MeV per nucleon, versus about 7.6 MeV for plutonium- 236).

check.html: Plutonium is large and unstable, consistent with being less tightly bound per nucleon.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 9: Carbon-14

question.html: <sub>6</sub> <sup>14</sup>C has a mass of 14.003074 u. Find its mass defect and binding energy.

body.html: Same hydrogen-atom method.

answer.html: Mass defect −0.113196 u; binding energy −105.4 MeV.

check.html: −105.4 / 14 = −7.53 MeV per nucleon, in line with Figure 6.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 10: Two pairs of nuclei

question.html: <sub>6</sub> <sup>12</sup>C and <sub>6</sub> <sup>13</sup>C; and <sub>5</sub> <sup>11</sup>B and <sub>6</sub> <sup>11</sup>C. How are the pairs alike and different?

body.html: Count protons, neutrons, and nucleons: C-12 (6 p, 6 n), C-13 (6 p, 7 n); B-11 (5 p, 6 n), C-11 (6 p, 5 n).
Same 𝑍 means the same element (isotopes). Same 𝐴 with different 𝑍 means different elements.
Pair 1 has equal proton numbers and different neutron numbers. Pair 2 has equal mass numbers and different proton numbers (B-11 has 6 neutrons, C-11 has 5).

answer.html: Alike: in each pair the two nuclei differ in neutron number and each pair shares one quantity (pair 1 shares 𝑍= 6; pair 2 shares 𝐴= 11). Different: pair 1 nuclei are isotopes of the same element with different masses; pair 2 nuclei are different elements (boron and carbon) with the same mass number.

check.html: Totals: pair 1 differ by one nucleon; pair 2 differ by zero nucleons.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 11: Tritium and helium-3

question.html: Tritium decays by emitting an electron and becomes <sub>2</sub> <sup>3</sup>He. Which nucleus has the more negative binding energy? Explain.

body.html: Example Problem 1 gives tritium: −0.009106 u, −8.482 MeV. For He-3 we need a mass; this is not in the book text, so we use the accepted atomic mass 3.016029 u (outside data).
Compare the binding energies from the hydrogen-atom method. He-3 has 2 p and 1 n.
Compare with −8.482 MeV for tritium.

answer.html: Tritium, <sub>1</sub> <sup>3</sup>H, has the more negative binding energy (−8.48 MeV versus −7.72 MeV). (This surprises many students: the decay occurs not because He-3 is more tightly bound, but because the He-3 atom has a slightly smaller total mass, 3.016029 versus 3.016049 u. In He-3 the two protons repel each other, which lowers the binding energy.)

check.html: The extra electric repulsion between two protons in He-3 explains the lower binding energy.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 12: Larger mass defect

question.html: Which of the two nuclei in the previous problem has the larger mass defect?

body.html: Mass defect is the mass equivalent of the binding energy.
|−0.009106 | > | −0.008286|, so tritium's defect is larger.

answer.html: Tritium (<sub>1</sub> <sup>3</sup>H), with a mass defect of −0.009106 u versus −0.008286 u for helium-3.

check.html: Consistent with the larger-magnitude binding energy.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 13: Strong force and large nuclei

question.html: Explain why in large nuclei the repulsive electromagnetic force can overcome the strong attractive force.

body.html: The strong force has a very short range, so each nucleon is attracted only by its few nearest neighbors. The electric repulsion has long range, so each proton is repelled by every other proton in the nucleus.

Adding more nucleons to a large nucleus does not add more strong-force attraction per nucleon (the number of neighbors stays about the same), but the number of proton-proton repulsions keeps growing roughly as the square of 𝑍.

answer.html: Because the strong force reaches only adjacent nucleons while the electromagnetic repulsion acts across the whole nucleus, the total repulsion grows faster with size than the attraction; in very large nuclei repulsion wins and the nucleus is unstable.

check.html: This matches the facts that all nuclei with 𝑍> 92 decay readily.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) 14: Heaviest nucleus formed by fusion in stars

body.html: Fusion releases energy only if the product has more negative binding energy per nucleon than the reactants. From Figure 6, this stops at iron-56 (𝑍= 26).
Beyond 𝐴= 56 the curve rises (less tightly bound), so fusing to make heavier nuclei would require energy instead of releasing it.

answer.html: Iron, 𝑍= 26 (iron-56).

check.html: The Lesson 2 text says the hottest stars fuse nuclei up to iron.
